assessment: The conventional control was faster on both successful calibrations and resolved two finite bounded cases where GCTS timed out. This configuration demonstrates no GCTS search advantage.
The negative control outcomes rely on the reviewed exhaustive algorithm and its saved exhaustion receipts. A separate, independently checkable refutation tree is not stored.

The backward control exhausted 2 completed catalogues within the declared line bound; GCTS reached its wall limit on those cases. These are finite-catalogue negatives, not proofs that the target statements are false or unprovable from the full axioms. Catalogue coverage and the line bound remain possible limitations.
Both search lanes benefit from the compact compiler. A GCTS-specific contribution still requires a measured gain from its markings or cluster search.

Lossless structural sharing and exact factorized candidate counts address the eager-construction bottleneck without deliberately dropping formulas, rule witnesses or row references. Source arguments cover the declared catalogue construction; fifteen exhaustive tiny models confirm its projection and graph behavior on those models. Tiny observations do not establish unrestricted first-order completeness.
The two lanes provide a concrete within-catalogue comparison. Any difference concerns these bounded inputs and implementations; it does not establish superiority over existing theorem provers.

A useful next experiment is a checked inventory of conditional cluster families. The same acquired lemmas and acquisition/invocation costs must be available to a conventional control. RL can propose instantiated clusters while the complete base-tile fallback and native checker preserve the validity boundary. No new RL training is claimed here.

Separate controls covered four resource refusals, detached/mutating and throwing observers, four data forgeries, and shared-premise proof bounds. The solvers each returned one witness where successful; they did not enumerate all solutions.
